newsitem.title: ROMANIA: New Romanian PM pledges reform, corruption fight.
newsitem.headline: New Romanian PM pledges reform, corruption fight.

text.p: Prime Minister-designate Victor Ciorbea, who won popularity as Bucharest mayor for sacking crooked city hall officials, has pledged to uproot what he says is endemic post-communist government corruption.

Ciorbea, endorsed for his new job within days of reformist Emil Constantinescu's presidential election victory, said in an interview with Reuters on Wednesday evening that his government would seek Western approval for tough reforms.
It would also press ahead immediately to join NATO and the European Union.

Ciorbea, 42 with a thick shock of hair, said he had tackled corruption head-on in the five months since being elected mayor, thrashing defeated leftist President Ion Iliescu's handpicked candidate, former tennis star Ilie Nastase.

That meant sacking within two months department heads and directors and dozens of other staff after providing evidence of abuses. They were replaced, he said, "on a non-political basis, on grounds of competence, or more to the point incompetence."

"Corruption has been more widespread in government than in Bucharest city hall," he said. "I am convinced we have to fight this mentality, this scourge, to turn Romania's government into a real democratic institution serving its citizens."

Ciorbea must be confirmed by the new parliament dominated by his centrist allies who threw ex-Communists out of government earlier this month for the first time in seven years. It meets for the first time on Friday.

He said he would pursue the "Contract with Romania" promoted by Constantinescu's Democratic Convention bloc -- a 200-day scheme of austerity measures tempered by increased benefits for those hardest hit by the transition to the market.
"There is obviously a big gap between us and the Czechs and Hungarians, made worse over the past seven years. For a time, tough but necessary measures will be taken," he said.
"But we also need to take steps to protect disadvantaged groups and ensure a decent standard of living for everyone."

He said the International Monetary Fund had requested talks in Bucharest next week with Constantinescu, himself and other leaders of the new coalition made up of the president-elect's Democratic Convention bloc and Social Democrats.
The IMF suspended credits this year after objecting to foreign exchange market practices and other policy problems.

"The essential changes brought about by the elections will...provide the credibility necessary for a real dialogue with the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and other institutions," he said.

A soft-spoken approach belies Ciorbea's experience as a trade union negotiator with ex-communist authorities and then his campaign for mayor on his own "contract with Bucharest". He is credited with clearing tens of thousands of tonnes of the capital's mounds of rubbish, providing cheap housing loans to young couples and free transport for students and pensioners.

He said he would be a "moderator" in bringing together "many personalities from different political parties" -- and blending into the government programme campaign pledges by former Prime Minister Petre Roman's Social Democrats.
"Perhaps that's why I was chosen," Ciorbea said. "I have spent much of the past seven years settling conflicts."
He said Constantinescu's victory would put the country firmly on the path of Western integration.
"We are totally oriented to the West. We have no nostalgia for the East...for the defunct communist regime and those who brought communism to Romania and eastern Europe," he said.
"It is our will to integrate in European and Atlantic structures and are taking all the steps to do so."
